stem:
A 41-year-old woman with biopsy-proven pulmonary sarcoidosis has two weeks of thirst, constipation and passing large volumes of urine. She takes no supplements. Her adjusted serum calcium is raised and her parathyroid hormone level is suppressed.

Which mechanism best explains the raised calcium?

options.A: Autonomous parathyroid hormone secretion from a single enlarged parathyroid adenoma
options.B: Activation of vitamin D by granuloma macrophages, independent of parathyroid hormone
options.C: Reduced renal calcium excretion because of chronic granulomatous kidney scarring
options.D: Increased bone resorption driven by a persistently high circulating parathyroid hormone level
options.E: Osteolytic bone destruction by widespread metastatic deposits within the skeleton

correct_answer: B. Activation of vitamin D by granuloma macrophages, independent of parathyroid hormone
why_correct: Macrophages in sarcoid granulomas express 1-alpha-hydroxylase and convert 25-hydroxyvitamin D to calcitriol without the normal feedback control. The excess calcitriol increases intestinal calcium absorption and bone resorption, so calcium rises and parathyroid hormone is suppressed. This is why a low or low-normal parathyroid hormone in a patient with granulomatous disease points away from a parathyroid cause. Source: standard teaching on granulomatous hypercalcaemia (sarcoidosis).
why_wrong: A. A parathyroid adenoma would give a raised or inappropriately normal parathyroid hormone, not a suppressed one. C. Granulomatous kidney scarring is not the usual mechanism; extrarenal calcitriol production is. D. A high parathyroid hormone level contradicts the suppressed result given in the stem. E. Bone metastases can cause hypercalcaemia, but nothing here suggests malignancy and it would not explain the link with sarcoidosis.
pearl: In sarcoidosis the hypercalcaemia is parathyroid hormone independent, so a suppressed parathyroid hormone with raised calcium should make you think of calcitriol-producing granulomas (or malignancy), and vitamin D supplements can worsen it.
thinking: Sarcoidosis with symptomatic hypercalcaemia  ↓  Parathyroid hormone is suppressed, so the parathyroid glands are not the cause  ↓  Granuloma macrophages hydroxylate vitamin D without feedback  ↓  Excess calcitriol raises gut absorption and bone resorption  ↓  Vitamin D activation by granuloma macrophages
exam_trap: A, a parathyroid adenoma, is a leading cause of hypercalcaemia in general, but the suppressed parathyroid hormone in this stem rules it out.
takeaway: Hypercalcaemia with a suppressed parathyroid hormone in sarcoidosis comes from macrophage production of active vitamin D.
notes: Rewritten as a clinical vignette with PTH suppressed given in the stem (angle: PTH-independent calcitriol mechanism; same key as source). Source key and explanations checked as sound standard teaching. No live PLAB 1 item tests the sarcoid calcitriol mechanism (searched sarcoid/calcium/calcitriol/1-alpha-hydroxylase; RES025 is sarcoid diagnosis only, END/CR items are primary hyperparathyroidism or malignancy). CKS not fetched.

stem:
A 66-year-old man with severe COPD attends a stable outpatient review. His arterial blood gas shows a raised carbon dioxide tension and a bicarbonate above the reference range, with a pH close to normal.

Which renal adaptation, developing over several days, accounts for the raised bicarbonate?

options.A: Increased urinary excretion of bicarbonate to counter the acidosis over several days
options.B: Greater tubular bicarbonate reabsorption with extra acid excreted as ammonium
options.C: Reduced glomerular filtration to conserve the circulating buffer in the blood stream
options.D: Suppressed ammonium production by the proximal tubular cells of the nephron
options.E: Decreased hydrogen-ion secretion by the cells lining the collecting duct

correct_answer: B. Greater tubular bicarbonate reabsorption with extra acid excreted as ammonium
why_correct: Chronic carbon dioxide retention lowers blood pH, and over several days the kidneys compensate by reabsorbing more filtered bicarbonate and generating new bicarbonate while excreting extra hydrogen ions, largely as ammonium. This raises plasma bicarbonate and brings the pH back towards normal, which is the pattern of compensated chronic type 2 respiratory failure. Source: standard teaching on renal compensation in respiratory acidosis.
why_wrong: A. Excreting bicarbonate would worsen the acidosis rather than compensate for it. C. A fall in filtration is not the compensatory mechanism and would not raise bicarbonate. D. Ammonium production rises, not falls, to excrete the acid load. E. Hydrogen-ion secretion increases in this setting, so a decrease would be the wrong direction.
pearl: A high bicarbonate with a near-normal pH in a patient with a high carbon dioxide implies chronic retention with renal compensation, whereas a low pH implies the compensation has been overwhelmed or the rise is acute.
thinking: Chronic COPD with raised carbon dioxide  ↓  Respiratory acidosis lowers pH  ↓  Kidneys respond over days, not minutes  ↓  They retain bicarbonate and excrete more acid  ↓  Increased bicarbonate reabsorption with more hydrogen-ion excretion
exam_trap: A, increased bicarbonate excretion, is tempting if the direction of compensation is muddled, but losing bicarbonate would deepen the acidosis.
takeaway: Chronic carbon dioxide retention is compensated by renal bicarbonate retention and acid excretion over days.
notes: Re-angled as a stable outpatient gas needing the renal mechanism (source was a bare one-line recall). Key unchanged. Distinct from CR001 (acute-on-chronic gas interpretation, tests diagnosis not mechanism) and PAAKT016. Standard teaching, no URL fetched.

stem:
A 72-year-old woman with COPD attends pulmonary rehabilitation because she becomes breathless on stairs and panics when it starts. The physiotherapist teaches her to breathe in gently through her nose and then out slowly through pursed lips, as if cooling hot soup.

What is the main physiological benefit of this technique?

options.A: It increases inspiratory flow so that a larger tidal volume is drawn in
options.B: It raises carbon dioxide levels to stimulate a stronger respiratory drive
options.C: It strengthens the diaphragm by adding resistance to every inspiration
options.D: It slows expiration and holds small airways open, reducing air trapping
options.E: It generates a rapid expiratory flow that helps to clear the sputum

correct_answer: D. It slows expiration and holds small airways open, reducing air trapping
why_correct: Breathing out slowly against pursed lips creates a small back-pressure that splints the narrowed small airways open during expiration. This reduces dynamic air trapping and hyperinflation, lowers respiratory rate and helps the patient regain control of breathlessness. It is a standard breathing-control technique taught in COPD self-management and pulmonary rehabilitation. Source: standard teaching in COPD self-management (pulmonary rehabilitation is recommended in NICE NG115).
why_wrong: A. The technique slows breathing and does not aim to increase inspiratory flow. B. It does not deliberately raise carbon dioxide and could not safely be used for that purpose. C. Resistance to inspiration describes inspiratory muscle training, which is a different intervention. E. Rapid forced expiration is the active cycle of breathing or huff technique used for secretions, not pursed-lip breathing.
pearl: Pursed-lip breathing is gentle and slow, with a longer expiration than inspiration; forced rapid exhalation is a different technique used for sputum clearance.
thinking: COPD with exertional breathlessness and panic  ↓  Breath out slowly through pursed lips  ↓  Back-pressure holds the small airways open  ↓  Less air trapping and a slower breathing rate  ↓  Slowed expiration with reduced air trapping
exam_trap: E, rapid expiratory flow to clear sputum, confuses pursed-lip breathing with huffing, which is a forced technique for secretions.
takeaway: Pursed-lip breathing keeps small airways open during slow expiration and reduces air trapping in COPD.
notes: Source asked only for the technique name; the vignette describes the technique and the question asks its mechanism (same learning point: pursed-lip breathing in COPD). No live item mentions pursed-lip breathing (searched). NG115 fetched but contains no pursed-lip recommendation, so the source line cites standard teaching.

stem:
A 61-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with sudden breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain. She takes oestrogen-containing hormone therapy and has an oxygen saturation of 94% on air. She had a deep vein thrombosis in her left leg two years ago. The clinician starts to apply the two-level Wells score for pulmonary embolism.

Which of her features contributes to that score?

options.A: The pleuritic quality of her chest pain
options.B: Her age being over 50 years
options.C: Her current use of oestrogen-containing hormone therapy
options.D: A previous episode of deep vein thrombosis
options.E: Her oxygen saturation below 95% on air

correct_answer: D. A previous episode of deep vein thrombosis
why_correct: The two-level PE Wells score includes clinical signs of DVT, PE being the most likely diagnosis, a heart rate above 100 beats per minute, recent immobilisation or surgery, a previous DVT or PE, haemoptysis and active cancer. A previous DVT therefore scores, and the total decides whether a CTPA or a D-dimer comes next. Source: NICE NG158, venous thromboembolic diseases, recommendation 1.1.17.
why_wrong: A. The pleuritic quality of the pain is common in PE but is not scored. B. Age over 50 is part of the PERC rule used to rule out PE in low-risk patients and is not a Wells item. C. Oestrogen use features in the PERC rule but does not score in the Wells PE score. E. Saturation below 95% is a PERC criterion, not a Wells criterion.
pearl: Wells PE and PERC overlap (previous VTE, haemoptysis, heart rate) but age, oestrogen use and low saturation belong only to PERC.
thinking: Suspected PE  ↓  Wells score estimates clinical probability  ↓  Score items: DVT signs, PE most likely, heart rate, immobility or surgery, previous VTE, haemoptysis, cancer  ↓  Age, oestrogen and saturation are PERC items  ↓  Previous DVT
exam_trap: C, oestrogen therapy, is a recognised VTE risk factor and is in PERC, so it tempts, but it does not score in the Wells PE tool.
takeaway: Previous DVT or PE scores in the Wells PE tool, whereas age, oestrogen use and low saturation belong to PERC.
notes: Changed angle from bare list recall to applying the score to a patient whose listed features include scoring and non-scoring items; key is a previous DVT (no threshold). Source AKT key was verified against NG158 table 2 (recommendation 1.1.17). Existing live items (CR024, CR044, ACU020, BX549) test next steps after the score, not its components. NG158 fetched.

stem:
A 68-year-old retired man spent thirty years working at an underground coal face. He now has several years of gradually worsening exertional breathlessness and a chronic cough. A chest radiograph shows multiple small nodular opacities, most marked in the upper zones, and there is no pleural thickening.

Which occupational lung disease is most likely?

options.A: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis from inhaled mouldy hay spores
options.B: Malignant mesothelioma arising after earlier asbestos exposure
options.C: Byssinosis due to repeated exposure to raw cotton dust
options.D: Coal workers' pneumoconiosis from long-term inhaled mine dust
options.E: Occupational asthma caused by sensitisation to isocyanates

correct_answer: D. Coal workers' pneumoconiosis from long-term inhaled mine dust
why_correct: Prolonged inhalation of coal dust causes coal workers' pneumoconiosis, with small nodular opacities, typically in the upper zones, and slowly progressive breathlessness and cough. A detailed occupational history is the key to recognising it. Source: standard teaching on occupational lung disease (pneumoconiosis).
why_wrong: A. Hypersensitivity pneumonitis is linked to organic dusts such as mouldy hay and is not related to coal. B. Mesothelioma follows asbestos exposure and presents with pleural thickening, effusion or a pleural mass rather than diffuse upper-zone nodules. C. Byssinosis occurs in cotton and textile workers. E. Isocyanate asthma causes variable airflow obstruction with a normal or non-specific radiograph.
pearl: Always take a lifetime occupational history in breathlessness; the dust determines the disease, so match the job to the pattern on the radiograph.
thinking: Long exposure at a coal face  ↓  Progressive breathlessness and cough  ↓  Nodular opacities in the upper zones without pleural disease  ↓  Coal dust is the cause  ↓  Coal workers' pneumoconiosis
exam_trap: B, mesothelioma, is the best-known occupational lung disease, but it is caused by asbestos and shows pleural disease, not nodular opacities.
takeaway: A coal miner with progressive breathlessness and nodular upper-zone opacities has coal workers' pneumoconiosis.
notes: New vignette with the radiographic pattern given; key unchanged and sound. No live item covers coal workers' pneumoconiosis (DT120 is silicosis with TB; RES024 and PAQ15445 are asbestos). Option distractor set re-worded. Standard teaching, no URL fetched.

stem:
A 71-year-old man who smoked heavily for fifty years has progressive breathlessness on exertion. He has a barrel-shaped chest, hyperresonant percussion and quiet breath sounds. CT shows enlarged airspaces and lung function testing shows a very low gas transfer. A pathologist later examines tissue from a lung resection.

Which pathological change is characteristic of his condition?

options.A: Permanent dilatation of the bronchi with chronic bacterial infection
options.B: Interstitial fibrosis that thickens the walls of the alveoli
options.C: Destruction of alveolar walls with loss of elastic recoil
options.D: Hypertrophy of mucous glands with excess goblet cells
options.E: Eosinophilic airway inflammation with reversible smooth-muscle contraction

correct_answer: C. Destruction of alveolar walls with loss of elastic recoil
why_correct: Emphysema is defined by destruction of the walls of the airspaces distal to the terminal bronchioles. Loss of alveolar tissue and elastic recoil causes air trapping and hyperinflation, and the loss of surface area for gas exchange explains the very low gas transfer. Source: standard teaching on COPD pathology.
why_wrong: A. Permanent bronchial dilatation defines bronchiectasis. B. Interstitial fibrosis causes restrictive disease with a reduced lung volume, not hyperinflation. D. Mucous gland hypertrophy is the feature of chronic bronchitis. E. Eosinophilic inflammation with reversible bronchoconstriction describes asthma.
pearl: Emphysema is a pathological diagnosis (alveolar destruction), whereas chronic bronchitis is a clinical one (chronic productive cough); both sit within COPD.
thinking: Heavy smoker with hyperinflation and low gas transfer  ↓  Hyperresonant, barrel chest  ↓  Alveolar walls are lost  ↓  Elastic recoil falls and air is trapped  ↓  Destruction of alveolar walls
exam_trap: D, mucous gland hypertrophy, is also a smoking-related COPD change, but it defines chronic bronchitis, not the loss of alveolar tissue.
takeaway: Emphysema is destruction of alveolar walls with air trapping and a low gas transfer.
notes: New vignette (CT and gas transfer wording, pathology question). Key unchanged. No live item tests emphysema pathology (RES043, BX133 and the alpha-1 antitrypsin items test aetiology). Standard teaching, no URL fetched.

stem:
A 74-year-old man has had three weeks of slowly worsening breathlessness on exertion. He has no fever and no chest pain. The left side of his chest expands less than the right. There is a stony-dull percussion note over the left base, and breath sounds there are very quiet.

Which investigation should be requested first?

options.A: Posteroanterior chest X-ray
options.B: Formal spirometry with reversibility testing
options.C: Diagnostic bronchoscopy
options.D: CT pulmonary angiogram
options.E: Transthoracic echocardiography

correct_answer: A. Posteroanterior chest X-ray
why_correct: Reduced expansion, a stony-dull percussion note and diminished breath sounds at one base indicate a pleural effusion. A chest X-ray is the first-line, widely available test to confirm fluid; thoracic ultrasound then guides any pleural sampling, and diagnostic pleural aspiration follows if the cause is unclear. Source: BTS Pleural Disease Guideline, Thorax 2023, and standard teaching.
why_wrong: B. Spirometry assesses airflow obstruction and would not explain focal dullness. C. Bronchoscopy is an invasive test reserved for later, once imaging and pleural sampling have guided the diagnosis. D. A CT pulmonary angiogram is for suspected pulmonary embolism, which does not fit a three-week gradual history with focal dullness. E. Echocardiography may be useful later for a cardiac cause but does not confirm the effusion.
pearl: Stony dullness with absent breath sounds at a base is an effusion until proved otherwise, and the chest X-ray comes before ultrasound, aspiration or bronchoscopy.
thinking: Slow breathlessness with unilateral basal dullness  ↓  Think pleural effusion  ↓  Confirm with simple imaging first  ↓  Chest X-ray, then ultrasound-guided sampling
exam_trap: Do not jump to an invasive or specialised test; a plain chest X-ray is the starting point.
takeaway: Suspected pleural effusion is confirmed first with a chest X-ray.
notes: Source key sound. Live BX266 tests the diagnosis from bilateral dullness in heart failure and CR062/RES018/RES031 test fluid analysis; none tests first investigation for suspected effusion. New vignette (man, gradual course, reduced expansion and stony dullness) with different options. BTS 2023 guideline cited as standard teaching only (not fetched).

presentation: Chronic cough and breathlessness in a smoker
stem:
A 62-year-old woman has smoked 25 cigarettes a day for most of her adult life. For two years she has had a productive cough each morning and now becomes breathless climbing a single flight of stairs. She has never been diagnosed with asthma, and her chest examination is unremarkable apart from a prolonged expiratory phase.

Which test is needed to confirm the diagnosis you suspect?

options.A: Resting 12-lead electrocardiogram
options.B: Spirometry following a bronchodilator
options.C: Sputum culture and sensitivity testing
options.D: High-resolution CT scan of the chest
options.E: Two-week twice-daily peak flow diary

correct_answer: B. Spirometry following a bronchodilator
why_correct: A long smoking history with chronic cough and exertional breathlessness suggests chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Diagnosis rests on spirometry performed after a bronchodilator showing persistent airflow obstruction (FEV1/FVC ratio below 0.7), alongside the clinical picture. Source: NICE NG115, Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in over 16s, recommendation 1.1.5.
why_wrong: A. An ECG assesses rhythm and ischaemia and does not demonstrate airflow obstruction. C. Sputum culture helps to guide treatment of an infective exacerbation but does not diagnose COPD. D. High-resolution CT is used to characterise suspected interstitial or structural lung disease and is not required to confirm COPD. E. A peak flow diary looks for variable obstruction and supports asthma rather than confirming COPD.
pearl: A normal chest X-ray does not exclude COPD, and a CT scan is not the diagnostic test.
thinking: Heavy smoker, chronic cough, breathless  ↓  Suspect COPD  ↓  Need objective proof of airflow obstruction  ↓  Post-bronchodilator spirometry
exam_trap: Do not pick imaging because the symptoms are respiratory; the diagnosis of COPD is physiological, not radiological.
takeaway: COPD is confirmed by post-bronchodilator spirometry showing persistent airflow obstruction.
notes: Source key sound. Live PAQ15631 gives spirometry in the stem and asks for the diagnosis, and GF046/GF048 test interpretation or treatment; none asks which test confirms COPD. Figure retained only as the standard 0.7 ratio (NG115), a long-standing cut-off and not the answer itself. New vignette (woman, 25/day, stairs).

stem:
A 68-year-old man who stopped smoking a few years ago has had a persistent cough and weight loss for three months. A chest X-ray shows a mass at the left hilum, and he has been referred on the suspected cancer pathway (an urgent, time-limited route to specialist assessment).

On examining his chest, which finding is most directly explained by the tumour narrowing the left main bronchus?

options.A: Painful swelling of the wrists and ankles alongside finger clubbing
options.B: Fine crackles heard at both lung bases at the end of inspiration
options.C: Swelling of both ankles together with a raised jugular venous pressure
options.D: A wheeze in one part of the chest that persists after coughing
options.E: Sharp pain in the side of the chest on deep inspiration

correct_answer: D. A wheeze in one part of the chest that persists after coughing
why_correct: A tumour growing in or pressing on a main bronchus narrows the lumen, so air moving through the narrowed segment makes a localised wheeze that persists and does not clear with coughing or bronchodilators. A fixed, unilateral wheeze in a smoker or ex-smoker should prompt imaging for lung cancer rather than a trial of asthma treatment. Source: standard respiratory teaching on central airway obstruction; NICE NG12 (suspected cancer, 2015, updated) recommendation 1.1.1 supports referral on the suspected cancer pathway when chest X-ray findings suggest lung cancer.
why_wrong: A. Hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy is a paraneoplastic effect, not a result of airway obstruction. B. Bilateral basal end-inspiratory crackles point to interstitial fibrosis or left heart failure, not a single obstructing lesion. C. Ankle swelling with a raised venous pressure suggests right heart failure, which is not caused by a unilateral bronchial tumour. E. Pleuritic pain reflects pleural involvement, whereas obstruction of a bronchus causes airway noise or collapse.
pearl: A localised wheeze that persists after coughing suggests a fixed obstruction, unlike the variable, widespread wheeze of asthma.
thinking: Hilar mass on chest X-ray  ↓  Tumour narrows main bronchus  ↓  Air through narrowed segment  ↓  Persistent localised wheeze
exam_trap: A paraneoplastic sign such as clubbing or joint pain is not caused by airway obstruction, so do not pick it for a mechanical question.
takeaway: Narrowing of a main bronchus by a central tumour causes a persistent, localised wheeze.
notes: Source learning point sound and not repeated: live PAQ15774, RES019, RES037 and PAAKT019 test SIADH, Pancoast and CT staging, not local bronchial obstruction (searched wheeze with cancer, central mass, lobar collapse). Vignette, options and framing rewritten with ex-smoker, suspected cancer pathway explained in-stem. Wording of NG12 recommendations checked on the fetched page.

stem:
A 72-year-old man with long-standing heart failure has had increasing breathlessness on lying flat for two weeks. His chest X-ray is reported as showing a homogeneous white shadow at the right base, with a smooth concave upper edge that rises towards the lateral chest wall and obscures the costophrenic angle. The trachea is central.

Which radiological abnormality does this describe?

options.A: Right lower lobe collapse with a sharply outlined triangular shadow
options.B: Right-sided pneumothorax with a visible visceral pleural line
options.C: Hyperinflated lungs with flattened hemidiaphragms bilaterally
options.D: Loculated lung abscess with an air-fluid level within a cavity
options.E: Right-sided pleural effusion with a meniscus along the chest wall

correct_answer: E. Right-sided pleural effusion with a meniscus along the chest wall
why_correct: Fluid in the pleural space tracks up the lateral chest wall, producing a homogeneous basal opacity with a concave upper border (meniscus) and loss of the costophrenic angle. Heart failure is a common cause of transudative effusions, and a central trachea fits a moderate-sized collection. Source: standard radiology teaching (chest X-ray interpretation).
why_wrong: A. Lobar collapse produces a triangular volume-loss shadow with the fissures or trachea pulled towards it, not a meniscus. B. A pneumothorax shows absent lung markings beyond a pleural line, not a dense basal opacity. C. Hyperinflation gives dark over-expanded lung fields, which does not match a white basal shadow. D. An abscess is a thick-walled cavity with an air-fluid level, not a smooth meniscus reaching the chest wall.
pearl: A meniscus sign with a blunted costophrenic angle on an erect film means pleural fluid.
thinking: Dense basal opacity  ↓  concave upper edge climbing the lateral wall  ↓  costophrenic angle lost  ↓  trachea central, no volume loss  ↓  pleural effusion
exam_trap: Candidates may call any basal white-out pneumonia, but consolidation shows air bronchograms and no meniscus.
takeaway: A meniscus-shaped basal opacity with a blunted costophrenic angle is a pleural effusion.
notes: Re-angled from a bare X-ray-sign recall item into a heart-failure vignette. Duplicate check: no live item tests the CXR meniscus/costophrenic sign (BX266 tests clinical signs of bilateral effusions in heart failure; RES018/RES031/CR062 test fluid analysis; RES024 mesothelioma). Content is standard teaching; no online source fetched.

presentation: PE imaging choice in severe renal impairment
stem:
A 66-year-old man with end-stage kidney disease managed conservatively attends the emergency department with a day of pleuritic chest pain and worsening breathlessness. He recently had a hip operation. He is haemodynamically stable, his clinical assessment makes pulmonary embolism likely, and the chest X-ray shows no alternative diagnosis. Iodinated contrast is considered hazardous for him because of his kidney function.

Which approach to definitive imaging is most appropriate?

options.A: Proceed to CTPA regardless of renal function, since a missed PE is more dangerous
options.B: Rule out PE with a D-dimer result, because imaging is unsafe in kidney disease
options.C: Consider a ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) scan as the alternative to contrast CTPA
options.D: Arrange transthoracic echocardiography as the sole test to confirm the diagnosis
options.E: Withhold imaging and treat empirically for pneumonia with oral antibiotics

correct_answer: C. Consider a ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) scan as the alternative to contrast CTPA
why_correct: When PE is likely, CTPA is the usual immediate test, but NICE advises assessing the suitability of V/Q SPECT (or planar V/Q if SPECT is unavailable) for people with contrast allergy, severe renal impairment or a high risk from radiation. This avoids iodinated contrast while still giving a diagnostic result. Source: NICE NG158, Venous thromboembolic diseases, recommendation 1.1.18 (checked online).
why_wrong: A. Contrast carries a real risk of further kidney injury, and NICE directs a V/Q alternative in severe renal impairment rather than ignoring renal function. B. A D-dimer is used to rule out PE only when PE is unlikely, so it cannot exclude a likely PE. D. Echocardiography may show right heart strain but cannot confirm or exclude PE. E. Treating as pneumonia without imaging leaves a probable PE untreated and delays anticoagulation.
pearl: Renal impairment, contrast allergy or radiation risk should prompt a V/Q scan as the alternative to CTPA.
thinking: Pleuritic pain after surgery, PE likely  ↓  imaging needed, D-dimer not appropriate  ↓  CTPA is the usual first choice  ↓  severe renal impairment makes contrast hazardous  ↓  V/Q scan
exam_trap: Candidates may reflexively choose CTPA or accept a D-dimer, forgetting that a likely PE needs imaging and that kidney function changes which imaging is used.
takeaway: In suspected PE with severe renal impairment, consider V/Q imaging instead of contrast CTPA.
notes: Same learning point as source (V/Q alternative in severe renal impairment); weak distractors replaced with plausible ones. NICE creatinine-clearance threshold deliberately left in words. Duplicate check: V/Q appears only in OG059 (pregnancy) and CR024/ACU020 (CTPA pathway); no renal-impairment PE imaging item is live.

stem:
A 52-year-old office worker is referred to the sleep clinic because his wife has noticed loud snoring with pauses in his breathing during the night. He walks to work each day and has never smoked. His recent thyroid function tests and resting blood pressure were normal, and his body mass index is 36 kg/m2.

Which feature of his assessment is the most important risk factor for his sleep-disordered breathing?

options.A: A body mass index well into the obese range
options.B: Normal thyroid function on recent blood testing
options.C: Regular walking to and from his place of work
options.D: A normal resting blood pressure on repeat checks
options.E: Having never smoked tobacco in any form

correct_answer: A. A body mass index well into the obese range
why_correct: Obesity is the most important modifiable risk factor for obstructive sleep apnoea, because fat deposition around the upper airway and neck narrows the pharynx and makes it collapse during sleep. Weight loss is therefore a core part of management alongside other measures. Source: NHS sleep apnoea information (obesity listed first among linked factors) and standard teaching; NICE NG202 (2021) covers diagnosis and treatment.
why_wrong: B. Normal thyroid function removes a possible contributor; it is hypothyroidism, not a normal result, that is associated with sleep apnoea. C. Regular walking is healthy activity and, if anything, helps weight control rather than promoting airway collapse. D. A normal blood pressure is not a risk factor; sleep apnoea is associated with hypertension as a consequence, not a cause. E. Never smoking is not a risk factor, whereas current smoking and alcohol before bed can worsen upper airway symptoms.
pearl: Other risk factors include male sex, increasing age, alcohol and sedatives at night, and anatomical features such as a large neck or enlarged tonsils.
thinking: Snoring with witnessed apnoeas in a middle-aged man  ↓  Ask what narrows or collapses the upper airway  ↓  Obesity is the dominant modifiable factor  ↓  Normal findings and healthy habits are not risk factors
exam_trap: Treating a normal result as if it were a risk factor, such as normal thyroid tests or normal blood pressure.
takeaway: In a middle-aged adult with snoring and witnessed apnoeas, obesity is the key risk factor for obstructive sleep apnoea.
notes: Re-angled from a bare one-line recall item into a clinic vignette, with distractors drawn from normal findings stated in the stem. Keyed answer unchanged and sound. Duplicate check: no live item tests obesity as the OSA risk factor (live OSA items RES022, DS015, DS016, PAAKT024, PAQ15794 test treatment, driving, investigation or diagnosis). NICE NG202 landing page fetched but the risk-factor wording was not verified there, so it is cited alongside standard teaching only.

stem:
A 44-year-old woman develops sudden breathlessness and sharp right-sided chest pain on breathing in, five days after an elective knee replacement. CT pulmonary angiography confirms an embolus in a peripheral branch of the right lower lobe artery. She then coughs up a small amount of blood-streaked sputum while on the ward.

What is the most likely mechanism of her haemoptysis?

options.A: Erosion of a bronchial artery by an adjacent tumour
options.B: Blood tracking into the airway from a ruptured oesophagus
options.C: Raised capillary pressure from acute left ventricular failure
options.D: Infarction of lung tissue supplied by the blocked vessel
options.E: Swallowed blood from a posterior nosebleed being coughed up

correct_answer: D. Infarction of lung tissue supplied by the blocked vessel
why_correct: A peripheral pulmonary embolus can cut off the blood supply to the lung segment beyond it, causing pulmonary infarction with alveolar haemorrhage. This produces pleuritic pain and small-volume blood-streaked sputum. Haemoptysis is a recognised feature of pulmonary embolism, and it features in the Wells score used to estimate PE probability. Source: NICE NG158, venous thromboembolic diseases (2020), and standard teaching.
why_wrong: A. A tumour eroding a bronchial artery would not explain an acute presentation after surgery with a confirmed embolus. B. Oesophageal rupture causes severe chest pain and vomiting with mediastinitis, not haemoptysis after a knee replacement. C. Left ventricular failure causes frothy pink sputum with bilateral crackles, and nothing here suggests heart failure. E. Swallowed blood from a nosebleed would be vomited or coughed from the throat, and the picture here is of a lung process.
pearl: Pulmonary infarction is more likely with a small, peripheral embolus than with a large central one, which tends to cause haemodynamic compromise instead.
thinking: Recent surgery with pleuritic pain and confirmed peripheral embolus  ↓  Small blood-streaked sputum  ↓  Blood supply to lung tissue beyond the clot is lost  ↓  Pulmonary infarction with alveolar haemorrhage
exam_trap: Assuming haemoptysis in a patient with a confirmed embolus must come from a second, separate cause such as cancer or heart failure.
takeaway: Small-volume haemoptysis in pulmonary embolism reflects pulmonary infarction distal to a peripheral clot.
notes: Source asked about the mechanism of haemoptysis in suspected PE; kept the same keyed mechanism with a post-operative vignette, confirmed peripheral embolus and a different distractor set. PAN4779 and PAN6912 test the identical learning point (PE haemoptysis = infarction) so only one is written. Duplicate check: no live item addresses the mechanism of haemoptysis in PE (BX265, BX144, PAQ15448, OG059 and CARD051 concern diagnosis, investigation or treatment). NG158 page fetched (Wells score includes haemoptysis); the infarction mechanism is standard teaching.

stem:
A 66-year-old retired plumber who has smoked for most of his adult life has had a dry cough for two months and now speaks in a weak, rough voice. Chest X-ray shows a left hilar mass with fullness of the mediastinum beside the aortic arch. Laryngoscopy shows the left vocal cord is paralysed and fixed.

Which structure has most likely been involved by the tumour?

options.A: Left phrenic nerve running over the surface of the pericardium
options.B: Right recurrent laryngeal nerve hooking round the subclavian artery
options.C: Left recurrent laryngeal nerve looping beneath the aortic arch
options.D: Left stellate ganglion lying at the apex of the left lung
options.E: Left hypoglossal nerve passing through the upper part of the neck

correct_answer: C. Left recurrent laryngeal nerve looping beneath the aortic arch
why_correct: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve branches from the vagus and hooks under the aortic arch, so a left hilar or mediastinal tumour (or involved nodes) can compress or invade it. This causes vocal cord palsy with a weak, hoarse voice, and hoarseness in a smoker is a red flag for lung or laryngeal cancer. A chest X-ray suggesting lung cancer needs referral on the suspected cancer pathway. Source: standard anatomy teaching; NICE NG12 (2015, updated) recommendation 1.1.1 for referral when chest X-ray findings suggest lung cancer.
why_wrong: A. Phrenic nerve involvement causes hemidiaphragm paralysis and breathlessness, not hoarseness. B. The right recurrent laryngeal nerve loops round the right subclavian artery, so a left-sided hilar mass does not usually reach it and the paralysed cord here is on the left. D. Stellate ganglion involvement gives Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis) rather than a voice change. E. The hypoglossal nerve supplies the tongue and lies in the neck, away from the mediastinum, so it would cause tongue deviation, not hoarseness.
pearl: Because the left recurrent laryngeal nerve passes under the aortic arch, left-sided mediastinal disease is the classic cause of lung-cancer-related vocal cord palsy.
thinking: Hoarse voice in a smoker with a chest mass  ↓  Vocal cord palsy suggests nerve involvement  ↓  Which nerve loops under the aortic arch on the left?  ↓  Left recurrent laryngeal nerve
exam_trap: Choosing the phrenic nerve because it also runs through the mediastinum, forgetting that it affects the diaphragm and not the voice.
takeaway: Hoarseness with a left hilar or mediastinal lung tumour points to left recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement.
notes: Adapted with a left hilar mass and fixed left cord so the item tests sidedness and anatomy (left RLN under aortic arch). Live PAQ15950 tests RLN palsy from a thyroid mass (different cause and site), so scenario and learning point differ. NICE NG12 and RLN course cited as standard teaching; no web page fetched. PAN4980 (same learning point) skipped to avoid repeating it within this batch.

stem:
A 58-year-old man has spent twenty years drilling and sandblasting granite in a quarry, usually without a face mask. He now has progressive breathlessness and a dry cough. His chest X-ray shows many small nodules in the upper zones and thin rim-like calcification around enlarged hilar lymph nodes.

Which inhaled agent is most likely to be responsible?

options.A: Asbestos fibres released from old building insulation materials
options.B: Coal dust inhaled during years of underground mining work
options.C: Raw cotton fibres inhaled in the preparation rooms of textile mills
options.D: Beryllium fumes released during the manufacture of metal alloys
options.E: Respirable crystalline silica released as rock is fragmented

correct_answer: E. Respirable crystalline silica released as rock is fragmented
why_correct: Crystalline silica from cutting, drilling or blasting stone, sand and granite causes silicosis, a pneumoconiosis with small upper-zone nodules and hilar nodes that may show eggshell calcification. Risk rises with cumulative dust exposure, and dust control and masks reduce it. People with silicosis also have an increased risk of tuberculosis and lung cancer. Source: UK Health and Safety Executive, Silicosis (hse.gov.uk/lung-disease/silicosis.htm); standard occupational respiratory teaching.
why_wrong: A. Asbestos causes lower-zone fibrosis, pleural plaques and mesothelioma rather than upper-zone nodules with eggshell calcification. B. Coal dust causes coal worker's pneumoconiosis, which also favours the upper zones, but the exposure here is rock cutting, not mining. C. Cotton fibres cause byssinosis, an asthma-like illness that is worse at the start of the working week. D. Beryllium causes a granulomatous disease resembling sarcoidosis, linked to alloy and electronics industries rather than stone work.
pearl: Eggshell calcification of hilar nodes is a classic radiological clue to silicosis, and these patients need to be alert to tuberculosis symptoms.
thinking: Years of sandblasting granite  ↓  Upper-zone nodules and eggshell hilar nodes  ↓  Pneumoconiosis from a mineral dust  ↓  Silica
exam_trap: Choosing asbestos because it is the best-known occupational lung toxin, ignoring the upper-zone nodular pattern.
takeaway: Stone, sand or granite dust exposure with upper-zone nodules and eggshell node calcification means silicosis.
notes: New vignette (quarry sandblaster, eggshell calcification). Live DT120 uses a stonemason with known silicosis but tests the TB work-up (key sputum AFB), so the learning point of identifying silica as the cause is not live. No web page fetched; cited as standard teaching.

stem:
A 72-year-old retired ship pipe-fitter has had over a year of worsening breathlessness on exertion and a dry cough. For decades he stripped old lagging from engine-room pipework. He has finger clubbing and fine late-inspiratory crackles at both lung bases. His chest X-ray shows lower-zone reticular shadowing with calcified plaques along the pleura.

Which condition best explains his lung disease?

options.A: Silicosis from inhaled quartz dust particles over many years
options.B: Asbestosis, a fibrosing lung disease from asbestos fibres
options.C: Sarcoidosis with chronic pulmonary parenchymal involvement
options.D: Malignant pleural mesothelioma with encasement of the lung
options.E: Extrinsic allergic alveolitis from repeated antigen exposure

correct_answer: B. Asbestosis, a fibrosing lung disease from asbestos fibres
why_correct: Prolonged heavy asbestos exposure causes asbestosis, a diffuse interstitial fibrosis worst at the lung bases, with fine basal crackles, clubbing and pleural plaques on imaging. It typically appears many years after the exposure. The fibrosis gives a restrictive pattern with reduced gas transfer. Source: NHS asbestosis information and standard occupational respiratory teaching; the occupational history is the key to diagnosis.
why_wrong: A. Silicosis causes nodules predominantly in the upper zones after silica dust exposure, not lower-zone fibrosis with pleural plaques. C. Sarcoidosis commonly shows hilar lymphadenopathy and upper-zone change, and neither the pleural calcification nor the occupational history fits. D. Mesothelioma presents with chest pain, effusion and irregular pleural thickening rather than bibasal crackles and reticular change. E. Extrinsic allergic alveolitis follows organic antigen exposure and often causes episodic symptoms with upper or mid-zone change.
pearl: Pleural plaques show past asbestos exposure but do not themselves cause breathlessness, whereas asbestosis does.
thinking: Decades stripping lagging with exertional breathlessness  ↓  Clubbing and bibasal crackles with lower-zone reticulation  ↓  Pleural plaques mark asbestos exposure  ↓  Asbestosis
exam_trap: Choosing mesothelioma because of asbestos, when the picture is fibrosis with crackles rather than pleural pain or effusion.
takeaway: Bibasal crackles, clubbing and lower-zone fibrosis after heavy asbestos exposure indicate asbestosis.
notes: Live PAQ15445 (asymptomatic pleural plaques, key asbestos), RES024 and PAAKT025 (mesothelioma) differ: this tests asbestos-related parenchymal fibrosis. No live asbestosis item found. Standard teaching; no page fetched.

stem:
An 82-year-old man with known heart failure stopped taking his furosemide two weeks ago. He is admitted with orthopnoea, weight gain and leg swelling but no fever or chest pain. A chest X-ray shows cardiomegaly with moderate bilateral pleural effusions of similar size.

What is the most appropriate approach to the effusions?

options.A: Bilateral ultrasound-guided aspiration now to exclude malignancy
options.B: Bilateral intercostal drains to relieve his breathlessness
options.C: Treat the heart failure with diuretics and review progress
options.D: Intravenous antibiotics for a presumed pleural infection
options.E: Referral for talc pleurodesis on both sides

correct_answer: C. Treat the heart failure with diuretics and review progress
why_correct: Symmetrical bilateral effusions in a patient with decompensated heart failure and no atypical features are presumed to be transudates. The best approach is to treat the underlying heart failure with diuretics and review the response. Pleural sampling is reserved for effusions that are unilateral or asymmetrical, associated with pleuritic pain or fever, or that fail to resolve with treatment. Source: standard teaching on pleural effusion in heart failure, in line with BTS pleural disease guidance.
why_wrong: A. Routine aspiration of both sides exposes him to risk without benefit when the clinical picture is clearly heart failure and there are no atypical features. B. Drains are for pleural infection, large symptomatic effusions or pneumothorax, and are not first-line for a transudate that will respond to diuretics. D. There is no fever, pleuritic pain or consolidation to suggest empyema. E. Pleurodesis is for recurrent malignant effusions, not for fluid from heart failure.
pearl: Treat first and tap later in bilateral effusions with clear heart failure, but sample if the effusion is unilateral, asymmetrical or fails to respond.
thinking: Stopped diuretic, orthopnoea and oedema  ↓  Bilateral similar-sized effusions, no fever or pain  ↓  Presumed transudate  ↓  Diuretics and reassess
exam_trap: Aspirating or draining both sides by reflex, when the clinical context makes a transudate likely and treatment of the cause should come first.
takeaway: Bilateral effusions in decompensated heart failure are managed by treating the heart failure.
notes: Adapted from N1946 (generic 'treat underlying cause'). Source stem was vague; angle sharpened to a decompensated-HF vignette with explicit atypical-feature caveat (unilateral, fever, pleuritic pain, non-response) per BTS teaching. Not a repeat of BX266 (diagnosis) or Light's items. Same vignette family as PAN4490 but different learning point (management vs mechanism). Guideline cited as standard teaching, not fetched.

stem:
A 77-year-old woman has long-standing heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and is increasingly breathless on exertion, with swollen ankles. Percussion is stony dull at both lung bases, with reduced breath sounds, and a chest X-ray shows an enlarged heart with small effusions of similar size on both sides. She has no fever or pleuritic pain.

Which mechanism best explains the pleural fluid?

options.A: Obstruction of a main bronchus by an endobronchial tumour
options.B: Spread of bacteria from the adjacent lung into the pleura
options.C: Leakage of lymph from a damaged thoracic duct
options.D: Increased capillary permeability from pleural inflammation
options.E: Raised capillary pressure forcing fluid into the pleura

correct_answer: E. Raised capillary pressure forcing fluid into the pleura
why_correct: In heart failure the raised venous and pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure drives protein-poor fluid across the pleural membranes faster than the lymphatics can clear it. This produces a transudate, typically bilateral and roughly symmetrical. Inflammatory, infective and malignant effusions are usually exudates and tend to be unilateral or asymmetrical. Source: BTS Pleural Disease Guideline, Thorax 2023, and standard teaching.
why_wrong: A. Bronchial obstruction causes lung collapse and may be associated with a unilateral malignant effusion, not symmetrical bilateral fluid in heart failure. B. Bacterial spread produces a parapneumonic effusion or empyema, which needs fever and a lung infection. C. Thoracic duct leakage causes a chylothorax, usually after trauma, surgery or lymphoma. D. Increased permeability from inflammation produces an exudate, whereas here there is no pleuritic pain, fever or inflammatory trigger.
pearl: Bilateral, symmetrical effusions in a patient with clear heart failure are almost always transudates caused by hydrostatic pressure.
thinking: Known heart failure with bilateral basal dullness  ↓  Symmetrical effusions, no fever or pleuritic pain  ↓  Transudate  ↓  Raised hydrostatic pressure
exam_trap: Choosing increased capillary permeability, which describes exudates (infection, malignancy, inflammation) rather than the pressure-driven transudate of heart failure.
takeaway: Heart failure causes bilateral transudative effusions through raised hydrostatic pressure.
notes: Adapted from N4490. Source option E 'Pulmonary embolism in every case' was an absolute-wording distractor; replaced with plausible mechanism distractors. Not a repeat of BX266 (diagnosis of effusion from signs) or Light's criteria items RES018/RES031/CR062/PAAKT020 (exudate classification). Pleural guideline cited as standard teaching; BTS/Thorax sites returned bot-block, so not verified by fetch.

stem:
A 69-year-old man has had 3 days of fever, productive cough and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. A chest X-ray confirms right lower lobe consolidation. He is alert and orientated, with a temperature of 38.9°C, pulse 104/min, respiratory rate 22/min, blood pressure 128/76 mmHg and oxygen saturation 93% on air. His C-reactive protein is markedly raised. The admitting doctor calculates his CURB65 score.

Which of his findings contributes a point to the score?

options.A: His age of 69 years on presentation
options.B: A temperature of 38.9°C on arrival
options.C: A resting pulse rate of 104 beats per minute
options.D: Right-sided pleuritic chest pain
options.E: A markedly raised C-reactive protein level

correct_answer: A. His age of 69 years on presentation
why_correct: CURB65 gives one point each for new confusion, urea above 7 mmol/L, respiratory rate of 30 or more, low blood pressure (systolic under 90 or diastolic 60 or less) and age 65 or over. This man is alert, with a respiratory rate of 22 and normal blood pressure, so of the findings given only his age scores; his urea is not yet known. Fever, tachycardia, pleuritic pain and CRP are not part of the score, so clinical judgement and oxygen saturation must be used alongside it. Source: NICE NG250 Pneumonia: diagnosis and management, 2025 (Box 2, CURB65).
why_wrong: B. Temperature is not a CURB65 component, although it supports infection. C. Heart rate is not part of CURB65 even though it is in NEWS2. D. Pleuritic pain is a feature of lobar pneumonia but does not score. E. CRP helps confirm infection and guide treatment decisions but is not in the score.
pearl: CURB65 is Confusion, Urea, Respiratory rate, Blood pressure and age 65 or over, and fever, pulse, saturation and CRP are not in it.
thinking: Consolidation on X-ray in a 69-year-old  ↓  Check each CURB65 item  ↓  Alert, RR 22, BP normal  ↓  Only age scores
exam_trap: Counting the fever, pulse or CRP because they look abnormal, although none of them is a CURB65 component.
takeaway: CURB65 uses confusion, urea, respiratory rate, blood pressure and age 65 or over, and nothing else.
notes: Adapted from N10448 (bare recall: which factor is in CURB-65). Built a vignette so candidate must pick the scoring finding from several abnormal ones. Source key correct; verified against NICE NG250 (published 2 September 2025) Box 2, which keeps the 2014 CURB65 definition. Not a repeat of Q357 (score calculation), ID019/ID044 (interpretation of a high score). PAN10449 (RR component) skipped as same learning point within this batch. Urea intentionally not given.

stem:
A practice nurse is teaching an adult with newly diagnosed asthma to use a handheld meter at home. He will record a reading each morning and evening in a diary.

Which instruction should the nurse give for each reading?

options.A: Breathe in gently through the device, then hold the breath for as long as possible
options.B: Breathe out slowly and evenly through the device until the lungs feel completely empty
options.C: Take a normal breath, then blow out steadily through the device for several seconds
options.D: Cough firmly into the device after a small breath, keeping the lips loosely around it
options.E: Stand upright, breathe in fully, seal the lips, then give one short, hard blast out

correct_answer: E. Stand upright, breathe in fully, seal the lips, then give one short, hard blast out
why_correct: Peak expiratory flow is the fastest flow achieved during a forced expiration that starts from full lung inflation. The patient therefore needs an upright position, a maximal breath in, a tight lip seal and a single short, forceful blast. The manoeuvre is repeated and the highest of three readings is recorded. Source: standard UK respiratory clinical teaching and respiratory service patient guidance on peak flow meters.
why_wrong: A. Peak flow is measured on breathing out, not in, and holding the breath has no role. B. A slow, complete exhalation is a vital capacity style effort and does not produce a maximal peak flow. C. A normal breath followed by a steady blow does not reach maximal flow and underestimates the true reading. D. Coughing after a small breath with a loose seal leaks air and does not reflect maximal expiratory effort.
pearl: Record the highest of three technically good attempts, at the same times each day, and use the same meter.
thinking: Peak flow measures maximal expiratory speed  ↓  Needs full inspiration first  ↓  Tight lip seal, no leak  ↓  Short, hard blast rather than a slow blow  ↓  Upright, full breath, seal, blast out
exam_trap: Slow, long exhalation sounds careful but is a vital capacity effort; peak flow needs a brief maximal blast.
takeaway: For peak flow, breathe in fully, seal the lips and blow out as hard and fast as possible.
notes: Replaces UN4686 (no live PLAB 1 item tests peak flow technique; searched stems for peak flow/mouthpiece/forceful). Source and live keys agree (full breath, seal, hard and fast blow); technique is standard teaching, not tied to a movable threshold. Not cited to a fetched guideline page.

stem:
A 58-year-old woman has had two days of fever, rigors and a cough with rust-coloured sputum. Over the right lower zone posteriorly, percussion is dull, breath sounds are bronchial and whispered words are heard clearly through the stethoscope.

Which change within the lung best explains these examination findings?

options.A: Air trapped in the pleural space, separating the lung from the chest wall
options.B: Fluid filling the pleural space and damping the transmission of sound
options.C: Overdistended alveoli with loss of elastic recoil and a barrel-shaped chest
options.D: Airway collapse behind a blocked bronchus, with no air entering the lobe
options.E: Air spaces filled with inflammatory exudate, so sound travels more readily

correct_answer: E. Air spaces filled with inflammatory exudate, so sound travels more readily
why_correct: In lobar pneumonia the alveoli fill with inflammatory exudate, producing solid lung that transmits sound from the large airways to the chest wall better than normal aerated lung. This gives dull percussion, bronchial breathing and increased vocal resonance or whispering pectoriloquy. The fever, rigors and rusty sputum point to an infective cause. Source: standard UK respiratory clinical teaching.
why_wrong: A. A pneumothorax gives a hyper-resonant percussion note and reduced or absent breath sounds, not bronchial breathing. B. A pleural effusion gives a stony-dull note with reduced breath sounds and reduced vocal resonance because fluid damps sound. C. Emphysema gives hyper-resonance, hyperinflation and quiet breath sounds. D. Lobar collapse from a blocked bronchus gives dullness but typically diminished breath sounds, because air cannot enter to generate or conduct sound.
pearl: Consolidation is the one common cause of dullness in which breath sounds get louder and harsher, not quieter.
thinking: Fever and rusty sputum suggest lobar pneumonia  ↓  Dull percussion means solid or fluid  ↓  Bronchial breathing and clear whispered speech mean sound is conducted well  ↓  Exudate-filled alveoli transmit sound
exam_trap: Dullness alone suggests effusion, but the preserved loud breath sounds and vocal resonance point to consolidation instead.
takeaway: Dull percussion with bronchial breathing and increased vocal resonance means consolidation.
notes: Replaces UN3955. Different vignette and a re-angle to the pathophysiology behind the signs (live CR009/PAQ16095/BX936 test CXR or diagnosis or management, none the exam-sign mechanism). Original key (lobar consolidation) is correct; no source error.

stem:
A 19-year-old man with cystic fibrosis attends his annual review. He describes a persistent cough that brings up thick sputum most days, and he has needed several courses of antibiotics for chest infections in the past year.

Which structural change is most likely to be seen on high-resolution CT of his chest?

options.A: Honeycombing with traction fibrosis confined to both lung bases
options.B: Dilated, thick-walled airways, typical of established bronchiectasis
options.C: Calcified pleural plaques along the diaphragmatic surface and chest wall
options.D: Pulmonary arteriovenous malformations scattered throughout both lungs
options.E: Multiple thin-walled bullae with a rim of normal lung at the apices

correct_answer: B. Dilated, thick-walled airways, typical of established bronchiectasis
why_correct: In cystic fibrosis, defective chloride transport makes airway secretions thick and sticky, impairing mucociliary clearance. Chronic infection and inflammation follow and, over years, damage the bronchial walls and cause bronchiectasis. High-resolution CT shows dilated, thickened airways, and a persistent productive cough with repeated infections is the clinical counterpart. Source: standard UK respiratory clinical teaching.
why_wrong: A. Honeycombing with basal fibrosis is the pattern of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and is not typical of cystic fibrosis. C. Calcified pleural plaques indicate previous asbestos exposure. D. Pulmonary arteriovenous malformations are linked to hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia. E. Apical bullae with a thin rim of normal lung suggest emphysema or primary spontaneous pneumothorax risk, not the airway damage of cystic fibrosis.
pearl: Think of cystic fibrosis as a cause of bronchiectasis in a young person with a chronic productive cough.
thinking: Chronic productive cough with repeated infections  ↓  Cystic fibrosis causes thick secretions and poor clearance  ↓  Persisting infection damages airway walls  ↓  Bronchiectasis on CT
exam_trap: Basal fibrosis and bullae are common respiratory CT patterns, but neither results from cystic fibrosis secretion retention.
takeaway: Cystic fibrosis lung disease is bronchiectasis from thick secretions and chronic infection.
notes: Replaces UN3860. Original was a recall item with a weak distractor set; rebuilt as a CT-pattern vignette. Checked live bank: BX259/BX911/BX260/PAN6185/DT082 cover CF malabsorption, diagnosis, inheritance, Pseudomonas and prophylaxis; none asks for the lung structural change. RES016/BX268 are bronchiectasis from a non-CF vignette, not CF. Key (bronchiectasis) is correct.

stem:
A 48-year-old man with long-standing bronchiectasis brings a tissue to his GP. It contains streaks of bright red blood mixed with sputum that he coughed up this morning.

What is the correct term for this symptom?

options.A: Haemoptysis
options.B: Haematemesis
options.C: Epistaxis
options.D: Melaena
options.E: Haematuria

correct_answer: A. Haemoptysis
why_correct: Coughing up blood that comes from the lower respiratory tract is called haemoptysis. In bronchiectasis, inflamed fragile bronchial vessels can bleed into the airways, so streaks of blood in sputum are a recognised feature. New haemoptysis in a patient at risk still needs a clinical assessment for its cause. Source: standard UK clinical teaching.
why_wrong: B. Haematemesis means vomiting blood from the upper gastrointestinal tract. C. Epistaxis means a nosebleed. D. Melaena means black, tarry stool from digested upper gastrointestinal blood. E. Haematuria means blood in the urine.
pearl: Haemoptysis is blood from the airway or lung, whereas haematemesis is blood from the upper gastrointestinal tract.
thinking: Blood coughed up with sputum  ↓  Source is the respiratory tract  ↓  Term for coughing blood  ↓  Haemoptysis
exam_trap: Haemoptysis and haematemesis are easily confused, but the first is coughed up and the second is vomited.
takeaway: Coughing up blood from the respiratory tract is haemoptysis.
notes: Replaces UN4499. Terminology item; no live item tests the term itself (live haemoptysis items test causes: mitral stenosis, TB, Goodpasture and similar). Note: it is a low-level recall item, owner may prefer to keep the live copy. No source error.

stem:
A 12-year-old boy with eczema has had a dry night-time cough for several months, with wheeze during football and when he stays at his grandmother's house, where there is a dog. His chest is clear between episodes and his symptoms settle quickly after a blue inhaler. His GP explains to the family what is happening in his airways.

Which process best explains his symptoms?

options.A: Fixed airway narrowing caused by long-standing destruction of the alveolar walls and loss of recoil
options.B: Thrombotic obstruction of the pulmonary arteries causing a ventilation-perfusion mismatch and hypoxia
options.C: Reversible airway narrowing driven by chronic inflammation and bronchial hyper-responsiveness
options.D: Progressive scarring of the lung interstitium that stiffens the lung and impairs gas transfer
options.E: Air entering the pleural space and compressing the underlying lung tissue

correct_answer: C. Reversible airway narrowing driven by chronic inflammation and bronchial hyper-responsiveness
why_correct: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory airway disease in which hyper-responsive airways narrow in response to triggers such as allergen, exercise and cold air. The narrowing is variable and reversible, which explains why he is well between episodes and responds to a reliever inhaler. This is why anti-inflammatory (inhaled corticosteroid-containing) treatment forms the basis of long-term control. Source: NICE NG245 Asthma: diagnosis, monitoring and chronic asthma management, 2024; BTS/NICE/SIGN asthma guideline.
why_wrong: A. Destruction of alveolar walls (emphysema) causes fixed obstruction in older smokers, not variable symptoms in a child. B. Pulmonary embolism causes sudden breathlessness or pleuritic pain, not recurrent trigger-related wheeze. D. Interstitial scarring produces progressive breathlessness with restrictive spirometry and does not fluctuate with triggers. E. A pneumothorax is an acute event with pleuritic pain and reduced breath sounds, not repeated wheezy episodes.
pearl: Asthma is inflammation plus airway hyper-responsiveness, giving variable and reversible airflow obstruction.
thinking: Recurrent wheeze with eczema and triggers  ↓  Well between episodes, relieved by a reliever  ↓  Variable, reversible narrowing  ↓  Inflamed, hyper-responsive airways
exam_trap: Fixed or progressive patterns (emphysema, fibrosis) and acute events (embolism, pneumothorax) do not fit symptoms that come and go with triggers.
takeaway: Variable, trigger-related airway narrowing from inflammation and hyper-responsiveness defines asthma.
notes: Re-angled from the diagnosis/mechanism item to a pathophysiology question in a child with atopy; checked against NICE NG245 (bronchial hyper-responsiveness is a diagnostic feature). No live item tests airway inflammation/hyper-responsiveness mechanism (searched hyperrespons, inflamm). Source key correct.
